19.0.0.en: Ahab reached his palace and met his wife, the wicked Jezebel, who nurtured and supported idol worship in the kingdom. He told her what had happened on Carmel: how the prophets of Baal failed to bring down fire from heaven, while for Elijah a great fire came down and consumed his sacrifice, so the people believed, and he seized all the prophets of Baal and slaughtered them at the brook Kishon. He did not mention to her the power of God that brought down the fire, or the inability of Baal to do so, and naturally he did not tell her how the rains poured down, because she had felt them herself, since they filled the whole kingdom. But why did Ahab not tell Jezebel about the power of God? This goes back to the following:

19.0.1.en: 1- His faith in God was very weak, in addition to his being affected by the killing of the prophets of Baal who were his followers.

19.0.2.en: 2- His fear of Jezebel, who nurtured idol worship, lest she become angry with him, especially since her personality was stronger than his.

19.0.3.en: 3- He may have come back to his senses after the uprising of the people when the fire came down and the prophets of Baal were killed, and begun to think that he had lost four hundred and fifty priests of Baal, and wanted revenge on Elijah and left that to his wicked wife; that is, he provoked her to take vengeance on Elijah when she heard of his harshness in killing the prophets of Baal.

19.0.4.en: 4- Perhaps he feared that Elijah would become a person of great standing, as Moses and Samuel were, so that the people would follow him and Ahab's position as king would be weakened.

19.1.0.en: Jezebel was greatly enraged when she heard of the slaughter of the prophets of Baal, and she expressed her anger by sending a messenger to Elijah, who was in Jezreel, telling him that she had sworn by the gods that she would kill him by this time tomorrow. This message means the following:

19.1.1.en: 1- That she was very angry and wanted to kill him, as she said.

19.1.2.en: 2- That she could not kill him because she feared the people would rise against her, especially after they had returned to God and come to know that He is the true God. But by this threat she wanted to frighten Elijah so that he would flee, leaving the field clear for her, and she could by her schemes bring the people back to the worship of her idols. This is the more likely meaning.

19.2.0.en: When Elijah heard Jezebel's threat, he sadly carried out her plan, or rather the plan of Satan, and fled quickly from Jezreel southward to Beersheba, which lies in the south of the kingdom of Judah, about one hundred and fifty kilometers from Jezreel. When he arrived there, he was in great distress and despair, so that he could not even bear to be with his servant; he left him there and went on southward into the wilderness to be alone.

19.2.1.en: Elijah's flight was the opposite of what God wanted, for the people had become ready for life with God, and he ought to have remained in their midst and encouraged them to hold fast to God's commandments and law so that they would be established in the faith. But his flight gave Jezebel the opportunity to bring them back to their old life of mixing the worship of God with idols. And the state of despair Elijah was in kept him from going to Jehoshaphat, king of the kingdom of Judah, in Jerusalem, to which Beersheba belonged, because in his fear he trusted no one with himself, not even the righteous Jehoshaphat, since he had become related by marriage to Ahab.

19.2.2.en: When Elijah looked at himself, he was afraid. If only he had looked to God, He would have taken the fear away from him, even though when he was with God he had not been afraid of King Ahab or of all the prophets of Baal who were with him. He is like Peter, who took his eyes off Christ when he was walking on the water, and began to sink.

19.2.3.en: You are mighty as long as you look to God, and demons tremble before you. But if you give in to your weakness, Satan will trouble you with his thoughts, and even draw you away from God and bring you into despair. Repeat a short prayer throughout the day so that you remember that God is always with you.

19.3.0.en: Juniper tree: a kind of wormwood-type tree that grows in the desert and gives abundant shade. Elijah left his servant at Beersheba and went southward on the road through the wilderness of Sinai, a day's journey. A day's journey means seven hours that a person walks in a day, resting during them, and in these seven hours he covers twenty miles. Feelings of sorrow had overcome Elijah for the following reasons:

19.3.1.en: 1- Bodily exhaustion as a result of what had happened two days earlier, when he offered the sacrifice, killed the prophets of Baal, and prayed a fervent prayer until the rain came; then he ran before Ahab's chariot until he reached Jezreel, on the day after that; then how he traveled a great distance from Jezreel to Beersheba; and finally on this day he walked seven hours until he arrived and rested under the juniper tree. This bodily weariness therefore also affected his state of mind, because of the difficulty of the events he had passed through.

19.3.2.en: 2- His fear of Jezebel's threat to cut off his head. Despite his faith and courage in confronting Ahab and killing the prophets of Baal, he weakened and feared Jezebel and fled, and some fear still remained within him that she would send a messenger after him who would kill him.

19.3.3.en: 3- His despair over the usefulness of his ministry. After he had succeeded in bringing the people back to faith in God on Mount Carmel, he was not able to lead them in the new life with God, because Jezebel had threatened him with death, so he fled, surrendering to despair and losing the sense of God's support for him.

19.3.4.en: 4- His sense of loneliness, that is, that he was the only one who still worshiped God, while all the people were behind Jezebel in idol worship.

19.3.5.en: 5- Perhaps he had become proud when God accepted his sacrifice by fire and he was able to kill the prophets of Baal, that is, he had achieved what no one else had achieved, so the devil afterward fought him with pride, which turned, after Jezebel's threat to him, into fear and despair. God allowed him this weakness so that he would be humbled and review himself in the quiet of the wilderness, but the merciful God would not leave him, as we shall see in the following verses.

19.3.6.en: He expressed his despair by asking for death, that he might be gathered to his fathers, and perhaps he then remembered the troubles that the earlier prophets such as Moses and David had met with, and forgot the power that had supported him.

19.4.0.en: After the toil of a long day, when Elijah felt weariness, distress and despair, he slept under the juniper tree. But God's tenderness could not leave him, because he was His son, even if he was in spiritual weakness. So He sent him an angel who touched him tenderly and woke him, and it was evening. The angel told him to eat, for he had prepared a table before him, that he might eat and be comforted and that it might bring him out of his sorrowful feelings. We notice here that God cares for Elijah's food in a wonderful and amazing way: when the famine began He sent him the raven to feed him with bread and meat, then He fed him at the widow of Zarephath of Sidon, and now He feeds him by means of the angel.

19.4.1.en: In the hour of distress, be sure that God is able to intervene in ways beyond understanding to rescue and sustain you. So be at peace, rely on Him, and seek Him with faith, whatever the troubles around you, for He will surely intervene.

19.5.0.en: Cake baked on the coals: a kind of large bread made by placing flattened dough on a stone made very hot by the sun, or heated by fire, so that the bread is cooked within minutes. This bread is well known and loved in the Arab regions full of deserts. This bread is also called the bread of the baked cake (Gen 18:6), which Abraham made for his three guests.

19.5.1.en: Elijah rejoiced greatly and was comforted by the sight of the angel and his tender touches. He looked and found that the angel had prepared the table by his head, consisting of a large cake baked on the coals and beside it a large jar filled with water. This bread tastes delicious, and it is a beloved table: hot food and plenty of water comfort a person sleeping alone in the wilderness, without food or drink. So he rose and ate much of this large cake and drank as much water as he wanted, then slept in peace in the hands of the angel who guarded him and cared for him, especially after his stomach was filled with food and drink and he was satisfied.

19.6.0.en: After Elijah had slept long enough under the angel's guard, which was probably the whole night, the angel touched him tenderly in the early morning for the second time (which means that he was under the angel's guard and care throughout the night), and woke him. After he had rested and the food he had eaten was digested, the angel told him to rise and eat a second time, because he would walk a long distance to reach the place he was heading for. For God, in His foreknowledge, knew that he would walk a long way in the wilderness until he reached Mount Horeb inside the wilderness of Sinai. This is a divine tenderness that surpasses understanding and surpasses a mother's care for her infant, because He cares for His prophet despite his sin and weakness, for he is His son before everything else, especially since Elijah had become alone, isolated from everyone, and found God with him, compensating him for everything. God showed man's psychological need for someone to share with him when angels came to minister to Christ after He had fasted forty days and forty nights (Mt 4:2, 11).

19.7.0.en: Horeb: a mountain in the wilderness of Sinai on which God appeared in His glory before His people, and to which Moses went up and received the commandments and the Law and the pattern of the tabernacle of meeting.

19.7.1.en: Elijah arose, ate of the bread and drank of the water while in the hands of the angel. We notice that God gave him the food that suited him, because he had grown accustomed to life in the wilderness and austerity; so He gave him bread and water only, although years before He had given him bread and meat, and afterward He gave him unleavened cake at the widow of Zarephath of Sidon, and now He gives him bread, because he had become accustomed to the ascetic life.

19.7.2.en: After that Elijah arose refreshed and strong, to walk a long distance in the desert until he reached Mount Horeb, which the Holy Bible calls the mountain of God. It is a holy place, indeed the holiest place in the wilderness of Sinai and its surroundings, and the Holy Bible does not mention that anyone visited it after Moses except Elijah; it is the place where the saints meet with God. The distance to Mount Horeb is about one hundred and sixty miles, and Elijah covered it in forty days, walking about four miles each day, which is roughly a third of the distance a person can walk daily. Perhaps he did this because he was in no hurry to reach the mountain, because he had forgotten fleeing from Jezebel and walked with God, because he was encouraged by the appearance of the angel to him. He may also have walked some days longer distances than four miles and rested on other days from walking.

19.7.3.en: And who made Elijah go to Horeb? There are two possibilities:

19.7.4.en: 1- That God guided him by the angel to go to this holy place, so that he might be strengthened and receive a spiritual and psychological blessing.

19.7.5.en: 2- That, since hope had begun to stir in his heart after seeing the angel, he longed to go to this holy place where God gave man the commandments and the Law.

19.7.6.en: But why did Elijah spend forty days fasting until he reached Horeb, when he could have reached it in about a week, or more, if he had walked a longer distance each day?

19.7.7.en: 1- It was God's opportunity to develop hope within Elijah and establish him through the quiet of the wilderness, the striving of the walk, and the remembrance of God's dealings with Elijah in the previous years.

19.7.8.en: 2- So that Jezebel's pursuit of him might be completely forgotten, and he might be occupied with his life with God in the quiet of the wilderness.

19.7.9.en: 3- So that he might fast the longest period a person can endure, which is forty days, as Moses fasted on the mountain. During a long fast a person forgets his own strength and rises spiritually, to feel God.

19.7.10.en: 4- So that he might remember how God preserved Moses and prepared him to meet Him on the mountain, and how the people came to Him in the wilderness for forty years so that they would forget the idols of Egypt and know God; that is, to remember that God alone is his helper, his refuge and his satisfaction.

19.7.11.en: 5- So that he might see how God sustains him for forty days without food as he walks in the wilderness, enjoying fellowship with Him.

19.8.0.en: When Elijah reached Mount Horeb, he found the cave into which Moses had entered when he asked to see God, and God hid him in it and passed by before him (Ex 33:22). The text says "the cave" with the definite article to confirm this meaning, and does not say "a cave", that is, any cave in the mountain.

19.8.1.en: After Elijah had slept in the cave and woken, he felt peace on this holy mountain, and he became strong and ready for God to speak to him and rebuke him. So He said to him, "What doest thou here, Elijah?", meaning by this several things:

19.8.2.en: 1- Why did you leave your work as spiritual leader of the people after they declared their faith? They need your guidance and encouragement so that they may remain firm in the faith.

19.8.3.en: 2- Why did you fear Jezebel, although I supported you before the wicked Ahab and you did not fear to confront him? Why have you fled now and come here?

19.8.4.en: 3- Elijah was accustomed to being led by God. It was He who sent him to the brook Cherith, where the ravens fed him (ch. 17:3-6), then sent him to Zarephath of Sidon to be sustained by the widow (ch. 17:9), and after three and a half years sent him to meet Ahab (ch. 18:1) and brought him to Mount Carmel. But here God did not command him to come to Sinai.

19.9.0.en: Elijah rejoiced at meeting God, with whose fellowship in the wilderness he had become familiar, and he hurried to speak to Him, to pour out all the pressures stored up in his heart and all his feelings of distress and despair, for He was his God and his only refuge. So he expressed everything within him and his weaknesses, and told God that he had been jealous for God's glory, because the people, led by the king, had turned away from God, and their wickedness appeared in the following:

19.9.1.en: 1- They forsook their covenant with God (to live as a people of His own), which they had made with God on Mount Horeb with Moses long ago. Now they forsook it and associated idol worship with Him, which God had forbidden in His covenant with them.

19.9.2.en: 2- They threw down and broke down the altars that the people of Israel had built on the high places for the worship of God, because they were far from God's altar in Jerusalem. Building these altars was a mistake, since the only altar ought to be in Jerusalem, but it was of course better than worshiping idols. So when Jezebel stirred up war against those who believed in God, she demolished these altars that these believers had built.

19.9.3.en: 3- The hand of the wicked Jezebel stretched out to kill God's prophets, who opposed the worship of idols.

19.9.4.en: Then in despair he said to God, "I, even I only, am left", although he knew that there were a hundred prophets whom Obadiah was sustaining, but they were hiding for fear of Jezebel. So he felt their inability to serve, and now here he joins them in despair and hides from the face of Jezebel. Perhaps he felt his failure to bring back even one person of the people to God, although this was not true, as we shall see from God's following words, in addition to the effect on many, whose faith would be completed with time.

19.9.5.en: In all this Elijah overlooked and forgot that God is the One working in his ministry, and not Elijah by his own strength, and that every step that takes place is used by God to complete His kingdom over the hearts of His children. By himself he despairs, but by relying on God he is strengthened and continues his ministry, even if the fruits do not appear quickly.

19.9.6.en: We also notice that Elijah, in his distress and agitation, did not answer God's question but poured out his suppressed feelings, and God listened to him in His fatherly love to give him rest. But it would have been better for Elijah to answer the question by declaring his repentance for his sins, saying: I have grown weak, my God, and feared Jezebel and fled here, and God in His tenderness would have forgiven him and guided him as to what to do. There was no need for the excuses that Elijah offered for his flight. He reminds us of Adam when God called him in the garden: he did not declare his repentance before Him, but offered an excuse, that he was naked, and then that the woman gave him and he ate. From God's meeting and speaking with Elijah, God's wonderful love appears in the following:

19.9.7.en: 1- God's steadfastness in His love, however man changes. It was He who called him to stop the rain, and sustained him by the ravens, then at the widow of Zarephath of Sidon, and supported him and accepted his sacrifice on Mount Carmel, and still has compassion on him in his despair at Mount Horeb. God is truly the Father who never changes in His love.

19.9.8.en: 2- God's love appears even more when man grows weak. He had sent him the ravens to feed him, then the poor widow in Zarephath of Sidon, but now for the first time an angel appears to him to feed him, because he is in greater weakness than before, so God's mercies toward him increased in order to rescue him, just as Christ after His resurrection sent a special message to Peter who denied Him, letting him know that He had risen, and likewise took him apart at the Sea of Tiberias after His resurrection and rebuked him to restore him to his first rank (Mk 16:7, Jn 21:

19.9.9.en: 3- God's longsuffering appears in the angel waking him while he was under the juniper tree, then waking him a second time and feeding him again, and after that in His being longsuffering toward him for forty days to encourage him and renew his hope, and finally in appearing to him on holy Mount Horeb, to begin rebuking him and restore him to his former strength.

19.9.10.en: 4- God's love appears in not rebuking the prophet Elijah when he fled from Jezebel, but letting him arrive in peace at Beersheba, then leave his servant and reach the juniper tree, and there feeding him twice by the hand of the angel, then caring for him until he reached Horeb, although God did not approve of his flight from Jezebel. But God's fatherhood has compassion on His children even during sin, and at the proper time rebukes them and brings them back to Him. God's love surpasses understanding, for He loves us while we are in sin, and not only after we repent, and He cares for us, so that perhaps His mercies may lead us to faith and repentance.

19.9.11.en: Look at God's love in your past life and how He cared for you, especially in troubles and above all when you were negligent toward Him, so that you may be ashamed and return and be bound to Him more, and thank Him at all times.

19.10.0.en: God commanded Elijah to go out of the cave to see God. For despite Elijah's lack of repentance and his mistaken excuses, God was not angry with him, but tenderly brought him out of the cave to appear to him and rebuke him and make him understand everything. It is a wonderful longsuffering with which God treats His children.

19.10.1.en: Elijah waited to see God, whom he expected to pass before him in one of the mighty forms that show His glory, such as the withholding of rain and drought, or the coming down of fire from heaven to consume his sacrifice. For Elijah had imagined, in the face of the evils of Ahab and Jezebel, that only mighty divine work that shakes the world was fit for the occasion. And as he was waiting, he felt a strong wind that rent the mountains, that is, a storm that shattered the rocks and moved them from their place, and he thought this was an angelic act announcing the nearness of God's coming, but God did not speak after that.

19.10.2.en: Elijah continued waiting for God, and an earthquake occurred that shook the whole place, and Elijah said to himself that this was a prelude to God's presence, but he heard nothing from God.

19.10.3.en: And after this he saw a great, strong fire appear before him, and he said to himself that our God is a consuming fire and will speak now, but he heard nothing.

19.10.4.en: We notice that these three phenomena are those by which God appeared to His people on the mountain in the days of Moses, when He gave him the commandments and the Law (Ex 19:16, 18). So Elijah imagined that these were the preludes to God's appearing, and because Elijah was zealous and fiery, he expected God's appearing always to be in a mighty, miraculous form. Finally Elijah heard a still voice, which perhaps he did not at first take notice of, but afterward he heard the voice of God, as we shall see in the following verses, so that God might confirm to him that spectacular works are not the only form of working, but God can work quietly and draw many to Himself. For Christ worked quietly and went about doing good everywhere, and He covered the sins of sinners, unlike Elijah, who is troubled and complains of the sins of the wicked king and people (v. 10). And in quiet work even unto death Christ gave us a perfect redemption. Indeed Elijah himself had quiet works that influenced those around him without his knowing it, for his life in the wilderness was an example to his generation and to the generations to come, in the love of solitude and virginity, for he is an early image of monasticism. And Elijah's steadfastness in his faith was a support to the hidden prophets and the seven thousand knees that still believed in God. God works in every way, so let us submit to Him and accept His ordering.

19.10.5.en: God appeared with a still voice that Elijah did not expect as a prelude to God's appearing, and God appears in our lives in many forms to which we pay no attention, because we imagine God according to our own desires. We have a clear example in Christ: when He became incarnate, only a few believed in Him, while the rest doubted and thought Him an ordinary man and not God. So in proportion to our reliance on God and our submission to Him we can discern His speaking to us through our daily life.

19.10.6.en: When you see problems in your home, or in the Church, or in any place, do not always think that the solution is a mighty divine intervention that troubles the wicked and shows your right. God may see that the solution is quiet work, even if your position seems weak, or you are accused by others. Do not hasten the fruits, for they will come, even after a while. Continue in quiet work and trust that God is with you and will never leave you.

19.11.0.en: Elijah finally realized that he was in the presence of God, so he hurried to cover his face, indeed to wrap it in his mantle, because he was in the presence of the great and awesome God, just as the angels cover their faces with their wings from the brightness of His glory. Then he heard God repeat to him the same question as before: "What doest thou here, Elijah?" And this means the following:

19.11.1.en: 1- That Elijah's first answer was not sound.

19.11.2.en: 2- The longsuffering of God, which gives His children many opportunities so that they may repent.

19.12.0.en: Elijah gave the same answer as before (v. 10), that is, his heart had not yet been moved to repentance, and he was still troubled, and thoughts of self and despair were fighting him, and he had not submitted completely to God.

19.13.0.en: The wilderness of Damascus: a desert lying between the region of Bashan and the city of Damascus.

19.13.1.en: Hazael: he was one of the officials close to King Ben-hadad, king of Aram (present-day Syria), and he killed his lord the king and reigned in his place, and attacked God's people and afflicted them greatly.

19.13.2.en: Jehu the son of Nimshi: he was a military commander in the kingdom of Israel, and he killed Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah and Jezebel and all the descendants of Ahab, and his descendants remained on the throne of Israel until the fourth generation.

19.13.3.en: Elisha the son of Shaphat: he was a farmer, and his father was a rich man from the city of Abel-meholah, which lies north-east of Shechem, and he was of the tribe of Issachar, and he took over the spiritual leadership of the people after Elijah was taken up to heaven.

19.13.4.en: God's love appeared in restoring Elijah to his ministry, for He said to him, "Go, return on thy way", and asked him to anoint Hazael king over Aram, and Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha prophet in his place. These three matters were only a calling and appointment from God and were not actually carried out until after Elijah's ascension, for the one who appointed Hazael and anointed Jehu was Elisha, because Hazael, being a pagan king, is not anointed with oil, whereas Jehu is from God and is anointed with oil. But these words of God mean restoring Elijah to his work as a prophet, though for a limited period, and Elisha would arise after him; for Elijah had made a great mistake by fleeing from God's work, just as Moses made a mistake and doubted God, so He barred him from entering the Promised Land, and as King Saul overstepped and offered a sacrifice in place of Samuel, so God rejected him and anointed David in his place.

19.14.0.en: God appointed three officials to protect His people from the wicked, for through the afflictions that would come upon God's people they would return to Him. So it is understood that Hazael would persecute God's people and kill many, that the rest might return to God; then Jehu would arise as king over Israel, and he would also kill the descendants of Ahab and the worshipers of Baal and his priests and many of the wicked, so that those who remained might repent. And if, after this, there were still a number of the wicked, the sword of Elisha would kill them, that is, the strong words of God that are in his mouth, for God works in various ways to bring His people back to faith and repentance. And these three are completely different from one another: the first, Hazael, is the head of a pagan state neighboring God's people, namely Aram; the second, Jehu, would be king over God's people Israel; and the third would be a prophet calling in God's name. So God works through the head of a foreign state from outside and through the head of His people from within, and the prophet was the voice of God in the kingdom of Israel, in which there is no temple of God, which is in the kingdom of Judah.

19.14.1.en: And these three did different kinds of work: Hazael was from the royal court, Jehu was a commander in the army, and Elisha was a farmer. That is, God can use all capacities for His service and for the repentance of His people. And by these words God reassures Elijah that He will remove evil, but not by his hands, but by means of others, these three; that is, he should not be hasty in carrying out God's judgments. So God distributed the service that Elijah ought to have performed among three. If Elijah had not fled, God would have used him, but God declares His pleasure with him by restoring him to anoint these men so that they may bear his responsibilities for him.

19.15.0.en: God reassured Elijah that he was not alone in worshiping God, but that there were seven thousand persons who worshiped God and had not bowed to Baal nor kissed his images, as was the custom of the pagans in their worship, bowing to the idol and kissing it. And this number includes the hidden prophets and other believers. God loves these, cares for them and knows them by name, although they were weak and hid in fear of Jezebel's persecution, while Elijah alone was the one who openly declared before the king that he worshiped God and proclaimed His name. So God has compassion on all and makes excuses for them, whether Elijah or the hidden believers. And the word "I have left" means that it was God who preserved these believers, even if some of them were weak and all that distinguished them was not bowing to the pagan gods. Elijah did not know them, since they were not distinguished, nor servants, nor helpers, and were not evident disciples of his, but they believed and lived a pure life in secret for fear of persecution.

19.15.1.en: By this God encourages Elijah that his ministry bore fruit in these seven thousand, so that he might be comforted and continue his ministry. And the number of seven thousand is of course a very small proportion compared with the total number of God's people, yet God cares for them and knows them one by one, and this encourages believers to stand firm in their faith, however many around them are far from the faith.

19.16.0.en: Yoke of oxen: a pair of oxen pulling a plow, able to plow an acre in about a day.

19.16.1.en: His mantle: a rectangular piece of cloth more than two meters long and less than two meters wide, resembling a cloak, which belonged to the prophets and was made of wool or hair.

19.16.2.en: Elijah's quick obedience to God appeared, who led him by the Spirit to the place where Elisha lived, so he went from the wilderness of Damascus, crossed the Jordan River and reached the city of Abel-meholah, which lies west of the Jordan River in the tribe of Issachar, and he saw Elisha. He probably knew him before, as one of the sons of the prophets or one of the pious young men who believed in God, so he did not need to get to know him. And he found him in his father's fields, overseeing the workers who were plowing the land, and his father owned twelve plows, pulled by twelve pairs of oxen, and this shows us how rich his father Shaphat was, because in one day he plows twelve acres, and of course he owned many times this number, that is, no less than a hundred acres, or perhaps more.

19.16.3.en: Elisha was careful to oversee the work in his father's fields, for his father had entrusted him with this work, and he was watching the last, twelfth plow in its plowing of the land to see that it was done well, so that the land would be fit for sowing afterward. He is meticulous and bears responsibility however great. And Elisha was probably a young man in his twenties, so that he could oversee this large work.

19.16.4.en: When Elijah saw Elisha he went to him and cast his mantle upon him. Casting the mantle meant Elisha's call to follow Elijah and be a disciple at his hands, to bear the responsibility of prophecy after him, just as when a man casts the mantle over a woman it means asking for her in marriage and taking her into his house, as in the case of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 3:9). Both of them are under the same mantle, that is, they become as one body in respect of work and responsibility. And so Elijah humbled himself and passed the prophetic work and the leadership of the people to Elisha, and since he humbled himself in this way he received a glory that no one else received, for after some years he went up to heaven in a chariot of fire. For when he was a shining star who withheld the rains and brought down fire from heaven, he was fought with pride and despair, so he fled; but when God rebuked him and he was disciplined in the wilderness, he became humble, so he received the greatest glory, and even appeared with Christ and with Moses on the Mount of Transfiguration (Mt 17:3).

19.17.0.en: Elisha rejoiced at Elijah's call to him to follow him and devote himself to the prophetic work and leave the management of his father's lands, and this shows how much Elisha loved God and his readiness to leave everything for His sake, for he ran after Elijah, that is, he carried out the divine call immediately.

19.17.1.en: But he asked Elijah's permission to kiss his father and his mother goodbye. Perhaps he was an only son with no brothers, since his brothers are not mentioned, and this makes it harder for the parents, that their only son would be consecrated to the service of God, in addition to their being rich. Yet they did not object to his consecration and did not hinder him. This shows that they were parents who cared for the spiritual life of their son and were submissive to God, and did not think of their love for their son in a selfish way that hinders the work of God, as some now object to the consecration of their children.

19.17.2.en: Elijah allowed him to return to bid his parents farewell and said to him, "What have I done to thee?", that is, it is God who called you and not I, and you have the right to bid your parents farewell, and you also have the right not to respond to the call. Perhaps by this he warned him not to be delayed by the customs of that time, in which they would spend days and weeks in farewells and their celebrations, lest he fall into the sin of postponement, which might weaken his desire for consecration, as Christ warned the one who wanted to follow Him but asked permission first to bury his father (Lk 9:59-61). And so Elisha left all his father's wealth for the sake of God, as Moses earlier left Pharaoh's palace for the sake of God, and as the disciples afterward left their work and followed Christ, and in the same way the saints did, such as St. Anthony and St. Paul, who left their wealth out of love for God and consecration to Him.

19.18.0.en: After Elisha rejoiced at God's call to him to follow Elijah and consecrate himself to God's service by means of the mantle that Elijah cast upon him, he wanted to express his joy at the consecration and his cutting himself off from the affairs of life. So he took a yoke of oxen, which was pulling one of his father's plows (probably he asked his father's permission for this), and slew them and made a feast for his loved ones and acquaintances, and used the wood of the plow to kindle the fire to cook the meat. Here it resembled a peace offering presented to God, that is, a sacrifice of thanks to God for choosing him and for his ministry. By this he announced to all that he was bidding them farewell to be consecrated in God's service, so that even thoughts of doubt, or the difficulty of the service, could not shake him and make him return to his former life, for this announcement was a cutting off and leaving of the old life to go on a new road that he would not leave. Then Elisha bade his parents farewell, and it seems that this farewell took only a little time, so he went and followed Elijah to be his disciple and serve him, as it is mentioned that he used to pour water on his hands (2 Kgs 3:11). And so Elisha began his consecration and discipleship at the hands of Elijah, and perhaps Elijah told him that he would be his successor in leading the people after a period of time, which increased Elisha's attachment to him and his care for discipleship at his hands, which lasted about sixteen years until Elijah was taken up to heaven, and Elisha took over the leadership of the people.

19.18.1.en: If God calls you to any spiritual work or service, do not be hindered by the affairs of life, and remember that Christ gave you His life on the cross, so whatever you offer Him is a small expression and a simple response to His love.

19.18.2.en: Ahab's victory over Ben-hadad and the pardon granted to him
